item.title: From Peer Pressure to Purpose
item.description:
Timely counselling, rehabilitation and behavioural support can play an important role in helping individuals overcome harmful influences, rebuild their confidence and return to productive livelihoods. Targeted support can also help beneficiaries regain focus, strengthen family financial stability and move towards a more disciplined and self-reliant life.
At 23, Prakash Londhe (name changed), a Scheduled Caste beneficiary from Nagpur, Maharashtra, was struggling with the negative…
item.content:encoded:
Timely counselling, rehabilitation and behavioural support can play an important role in helping individuals overcome harmful influences, rebuild their confidence and return to productive livelihoods. Targeted support can also help beneficiaries regain focus, strengthen family financial stability and move towards a more disciplined and self-reliant life.

At 23, Prakash Londhe (name changed), a Scheduled Caste beneficiary from Nagpur, Maharashtra, was struggling with the negative influence of a peer group. The situation affected his routine and distracted him from his auto-rickshaw business, resulting in irregular working hours, missed peak-hour commuters, poor daily earnings and financial instability. His family was deeply concerned about his future and the economic difficulties caused by his inconsistent income.

Seeking to break free from harmful habits and regain focus on his livelihood, Shri Londhe received support under the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) at Navjeevan Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addict, Nagpur, an Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA). The intervention provided professional psychological counselling, motivational sessions, behavioural support, rehabilitation assistance and peer-refusal training to help him resist negative influences.

Through counselling and behavioural support, Shri Prakash developed greater awareness of the harmful effects of bad company and substance abuse. With continued guidance and emotional support from his family, he successfully cut ties with the negative peer group and adopted a more disciplined routine. He is now focused on operating his auto-rickshaw business regularly and making better use of peak-hour demand.

By working full-time and targeting peak rush hours, Prakash Londhe has seen a significant improvement in his daily rides and income. The improvement has helped stabilise his family’s financial condition and strengthened his confidence in pursuing his livelihood.

Prakash Londhe’s journey demonstrates how counselling, rehabilitation and family support can help an individual overcome negative influences, regain focus and move towards greater economic self-reliance. His experience reflects the importance of timely support under NAPDDR in enabling beneficiaries to rebuild their lives with discipline, dignity and renewed purpose.

*****

SS-112-TAR/KV/GA/MK

item.title: From Financial Assistance to Self-Reliance
item.description:

Targeted support can also help beneficiaries turn their entrepreneurial aspirations into viable income-generating activities.
Smt Kavita Verma, a native resident of Sehore district, Madhya Pradesh, aspired to establish a sustainable livelihood and contribute to the economic well-being of her…
item.content:encoded:
Timely financial assistance can play an important role in helping individuals establish sustainable livelihoods, strengthen family financial stability and move towards economic self-reliance. Targeted support can also help beneficiaries turn their entrepreneurial aspirations into viable income-generating activities.

Smt Kavita Verma, a native resident of Sehore district, Madhya Pradesh, aspired to establish a sustainable livelihood and contribute to the economic well-being of her family. Limited financial resources, however, posed a challenge in starting her own enterprise.

In 2024, under the NSFDC Refinance Scheme, Smt Verma received financial assistance of Rs. 3,42,000 through Madhya Pradesh Gramin Bank, Sehore, Mandi Branch, to establish a Flour Mill (atta chakki).

With the financial assistance, Kavita successfully started her flour mill business. The enterprise created a sustainable source of income for her and helped strengthen the economic condition of her family.

Today, Smt Kavita Verma is successfully operating her flour mill business. Her journey demonstrates how timely financial support can enable self-employment, strengthen household livelihoods and help beneficiaries move towards greater economic self-reliance.

Kavita Verma’s experience reflects the impact of financial assistance under the NSFDC Refinance Scheme in enabling beneficiaries to establish viable enterprises and build a more secure and self-reliant future.

item.title: India Mining Week 2026 Brings Together Diplomatic Missions from 19 Countries for ‘India Mining: Global Connect’
item.description:
India Mining Week 2026, India’s largest conference-cum-exhibition for the mining and minerals sector, hosted ‘India Mining: Global Connect’ , an international outreach interaction that brought together representatives of diplomatic missions from 19 countries to discuss opportunities for greater international participation and collaboration in India’s mining and minerals sector.
The interaction was organised as part of the build-up to India Mining Week 2026 , scheduled from 15-17…
item.content:encoded:
India Mining Week 2026, India’s largest conference-cum-exhibition for the mining and minerals sector, hosted ‘India Mining: Global Connect’, an international outreach interaction that brought together representatives of diplomatic missions from 19 countries to discuss opportunities for greater international participation and collaboration in India’s mining and minerals sector.

The interaction was organised as part of the build-up to India Mining Week 2026, scheduled from 15-17 November 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, by the Ministry of Coal and Ministry of Mines, Government of India, in association with the mining industry.

The interaction was hosted by Shri Satish Chandra Dubey, Minister of State for Coal and Mines and Smt. Rupinder Brar, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Coal. Senior representatives from the participating diplomatic missions, along with stakeholders from the mining and minerals ecosystem, discussed opportunities for country-level engagement at India Mining Week 2026.

Shri Satish Chandra Dubey, Minister of State for Coal and Mines, called for active cooperation and participation from the global mining community in India Mining Week 2026. He invited partner countries to facilitate the participation of leading mining companies, major investors and prominent delegates, emphasising that such engagement would be mutually beneficial and further strengthen opportunities for collaboration in the mining and minerals sector.

He also expressed his keen interest in ensuring wide international participation, including the participation of Ministers responsible for mining from partner countries, as well as leading investors and industry representatives. He extended a warm invitation to all the dignitaries and stakeholders to join the inaugural event of India Mining Week 2026 on 15 November at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi.

Addressing the gathering at the India Mining: Global Connect, Smt. Rupinder Brar, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Coal, invoked the timeless Indian ethos of “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam”, highlighting the spirit of partnership and collaboration that can shape the future of the global mining sector. As India advances as the world’s fourth-largest economy, the mining and minerals sector has a significant role to play in supporting the country’s growth and global ambitions. With India Mining Week 2026 coming up in November, she invited the global mining community to come together, exchange ideas, share expertise and explore opportunities for collaboration. Ms Brar emphasised that India looks forward to the ideas, experience and support of partners from across the world in shaping a more innovative, sustainable and globally connected mining sector.

Representatives from Malawi, Sri Lanka, Mozambique, Algeria, United States of America, Chile, Bhutan, Indonesia, Ethiopia, Russia, Iraq, Morocco, Venezuela, Spain, Poland, Mongolia, Zambia, France, Ghana and US Chamber of Commerce participated in the interaction.

The discussions covered potential participation through country delegations, government and institutional representation, business delegations, speakers, technical experts, mining and mineral companies, technology providers, equipment manufacturers, investors, research institutions and industry associations.

The interaction also provided an opportunity to share the scope and programme of India Mining Week 2026 and discuss areas of mutual interest across critical minerals, mineral exploration, mining technology, heavy mining equipment, innovation, investment, trade and resource development. Participating missions were invited to facilitate the participation of relevant companies, government agencies, institutions and industry bodies from their respective countries.

With India expanding its focus on critical minerals, resource security, infrastructure development and domestic manufacturing, international cooperation is becoming increasingly relevant across the mining value chain. India Mining Week 2026 will provide a platform for countries and companies to present their capabilities, explore business opportunities and engage with Indian policymakers, mining companies, investors and technology providers.

The three-day India Mining Week 2026 will bring together 25,000+ industry professionals and decision-makers, 500+ exhibitors and technology providers, 200+ speakers and industry experts, 100+ conference sessions and technical presentations, 1,000+ government and PSU delegates and 300+ mining and mineral companies, with participation expected from more than 50 countries.

The event will feature a high-level conference, international exhibition, technical sessions, leadership dialogues, B2B meetings, technology demonstrations and product launches, with discussions spanning coal, metals, critical minerals, exploration, mining technology, automation, mine safety, sustainability, mineral processing and resource efficiency.

The ‘India Mining: Global Connect’ interaction is part of the international outreach programme leading up to India Mining Week 2026, with further engagement planned with international governments, mining companies, technology providers, investors and industry organisations in the run-up to the November summit.

For more information about India Mining Week 2026, please visit

https://www.indiaminingweek.org/

item.description:

The programme will mark the culmination of year-long celebrations that commenced on October 1 last year, commemorating 100 years since the establishment of the UPSC in 1926. On the occasion, Prime Minister will release a UPSC Centenary Commemorative…
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi will participate in the Centenary Celebrations of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) on October 1, 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi at 11 AM. He will also address the gathering on the occasion.

The programme will mark the culmination of year-long celebrations that commenced on October 1 last year, commemorating 100 years since the establishment of the UPSC in 1926. On the occasion, Prime Minister will release a UPSC Centenary Commemorative Coin, a Commemorative Stamp and a Book titled ‘100 Landmark Judgements- Shaping the Policies of UPSC and Public Service Commissions in India’.

The programme will witness participation of stakeholders from across the country, including Chairmen and Members of State Public Service Commissions, senior officers of Government of India, academicians, UPSC officials and others.

This event is part of the two day programme being held by UPSC on September 30 and October 1, 2026. The first day will feature ‘Shatabdi Samaroh - Manthan’ at Bharat Mandapam and will witness addresses by eminent speakers followed by panel discussions on various themes.

item.content:encoded:
Indian Coast Guard (ICG), in coordination with the Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), Gujarat, neutralized a major maritime narcotic smuggling attempt worth over Rs 3,000 crores in the Arabian Sea, west of Lakshadweep, on September 25, 2026.

The joint operation led to the seizure of approximately 526 kg of high-grade narcotic substances, including heroin and methamphetamine, and the apprehension of five Pakistani nationals who were operating the vessel.

 Acting on intelligence, ICG assets undertook precise sea-air surveillance and persistent tracking of the suspected vessel before launching a coordinated hot pursuit. The operation culminated in the interception and boarding of a suspicious Iranian dhow in the high seas.

The intercepted dhow, apprehended crew and seized contraband were subsequently escorted under armed security to Mumbai for joint interrogation and further investigation, followed by comprehensive multi-agency legal proceedings.

The successful operation represents a significant contribution to the national vision of a ‘Nasha Mukt Bharat’ and underscores ICG’s commitment to combating maritime narcotics trafficking and maintaining zero tolerance towards illicit activities in India’s maritime zones.

 ***

SR/Kamlesh­­

item.title: Beyond Cleanliness: The Women and Transgender Changemakers of Swachhata
item.description: A clean city is often noticed through what is no longer visible. Waste no longer lies on the street. Drains no longer remain clogged. Sanitation facilities are available when they are needed. But behind this visible change are journeys that deserve to be seen too. They are the journeys of women creating livelihoods from waste, leading cleanliness efforts in their communities and turning everyday challenges into opportunities. Alongside them are transgender community members finding…
item.content:encoded:
A clean city is often noticed through what is no longer visible. Waste no longer lies on the street. Drains no longer remain clogged. Sanitation facilities are available when they are needed. But behind this visible change are journeys that deserve to be seen too. They are the journeys of women creating livelihoods from waste, leading cleanliness efforts in their communities and turning everyday challenges into opportunities. Alongside them are transgender community members finding professional roles and recognition in sanitation services. Across cities, Swachhata is becoming more than a public service. It is becoming a space for dignity, enterprise, participation and opportunity.

This spirit of participation finds a national platform in Swachhata Hi Seva 2026, launched on 17 September 2026. Every year, the campaign brings citizens, institutions and leadership together to strengthen voluntarism and collective action for Swachhata.

With the theme “Swachhata Mein Sahbhag; Swachh Bharat, Viksit Bharat”, Swachhata Hi Seva 2026 places shared responsibility at the heart of the cleanliness movement. It underlines that the vision of a Swachh and Viksit Bharat calls for a Whole-of-Government and Whole-of-Society approach.

Such a collective spirit finds a meaningful expression in Loni, Uttar Pradesh, where something once treated as waste is becoming a source of livelihood.

When Waste Becomes a Livelihood

Around gaushalas and dairies, cow dung can become a difficult waste-management challenge, clogging drains and sewage channels. In Krishna Vihar Colony of Loni, however, a group of women saw a different way forward. They began using cow dung to make incense sticks and Loban cups.

What started with just 8-10 women grew into a livelihood opportunity for many more. A woman officer of the Loni Nagar Palika Parishad saw the potential in their work and helped connect the producers with gaushala owners for steady supply and utilization of cow dung. A simple idea began to take root: what if something treated as waste could be given another life?

During the summer months when incense production is at its peak, the initiative employs around 40-50 women. For these women, the work is more than making a product. It brings together livelihood, dignity, and the satisfaction of turning waste into something useful. The Nagar Palika Parishad also earns up to 25 per cent revenue from the sale of these products. This creates a link between waste management, local enterprise, and municipal revenue.

The products themselves carry the story of reuse. Traditionally, making incense products requires wood sawdust as the base material. Mixing around 30-35 per cent dry cow dung powder reduces the quantity of wood sawdust required. This has emerged as an environmentally sustainable solution that also ensures swachchta

What began in one colony has travelled much farther. The products are supplied to several parts of the country, including Delhi, Mumbai, Punjab, Gujarat and Hyderabad. During the COVID period, they were also produced for major brands, with orders reaching Mauritius and South Africa.

And the women are not stopping there. Plans are being explored to make combustible wood as fuel from cow dung for use in cremation grounds, havans, and other activities. The initiative is also exploring cow-dung flower pots that can eventually return to the soil as manure.

Here, the idea of cleanliness extends beyond removing waste. It means asking what else that waste can become.

From Waste Collectors to Waste Leaders

A similar spirit can be seen in Patna, Bihar, where women are breaking old conventions and giving cleanliness a new, inclusive face. At the city’s Pink Material Recovery Facility (MRF), women stand at the heart of the waste-management process. Operated primarily by women and led by a female supervisor, the facility processes dry and wet waste. It can manage 2 tonnes of dry waste and 1.5 tonnes of wet waste every day.

The idea for the Pink MRF emerged from an effort to create opportunities for women in the waste-management sector. The project team approached the Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC) with the idea of establishing a Pink MRF. PMC supported the idea, and the facility was set up in just three months. Its distinctive colour and design also drew the attention of local people, helping create awareness around the initiative.

The idea reaches the community through the ‘Cash for Waste’ initiative. Citizens can bring dry waste and receive payment at prescribed rates. Waste gains value, citizens gain an incentive to participate, and the city gains another set of hands in its cleanliness journey.

Patna’s Swachhta journey then takes an interesting turn. Old, unusable vehicles have been given a second life as mobile Pink Toilets. What once stood as scrap now serves a vital sanitation need. It is the spirit of the 3Rs: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle, made visible on the streets.

Together, the Pink MRF and mobile Pink Toilets reflect social justice, environmental awareness and economic opportunity. Above all, they carry a simple message: when women are given space in Swachhta, they do not merely become part of the system. They help reshape it.

Women Who Carry Cleanliness into Their Communities

The story of women and Swachhta does not end with the waste they handle. It grows through the communities they touch. In Bhopal, a group of 250 women brand ambassadors has worked with the municipal corporation on cleanliness and waste management. The group members have also established ‘Bartan Banks’ across 25 wards to eliminate the use of single-use plastic. By providing reusable utensil sets for community functions and events, these banks ensure that local gatherings are organized under zero-waste principles.

The 60-member ‘Swachhata Kitty Group’ has found another way to turn togetherness into action. Each woman contributes ₹100 every month, creating a shared pool for community cleanliness activities. Small contributions, carried by many hands, become a collective commitment to a cleaner neighbourhood.

In Uttarakhand, this spirit has taken the name ‘Bainni Sena ’-the ‘Army of Sisters’. Across 57 groups, 570 women monitor cleanliness activities in their wards. They interact with citizens, help communicate complaints, conduct awareness programmes, and support coordination between the municipal administration and sanitation workers. Their work happens where a city’s cleanliness is truly decided. It takes shape in neighbourhoods, in conversations and in the small moments when someone chooses to care.

In Shillong, the Iynnehskhem Self-Help Group has found a new path to livelihood through waste. The women collect wet waste from homes and turn biodegradable waste into compost. Once involved in waste picking, they received training through a rehabilitation initiative and built a new livelihood around composting. Their unity earned them the affectionate name ‘Meri Maidens of Marton’.

Through their everyday efforts, the women are turning Swachhta from a responsibility into a shared culture of care.

When Inclusion Changes the Face of Sanitation

In Odisha, transgender persons are taking on roles that place them at the heart of urban sanitation systems. The change began in Cuttack, where the Municipal Corporation organised transgender persons into a Self-Help Group. They were trained and entrusted with the operation and maintenance of a Septage Treatment Plant.

It was a significant shift. A community that has often faced exclusion from formal opportunities was now taking responsibility for a technical sanitation facility.

The model subsequently expanded across Odisha. Urban Local Bodies began partnering with Self-Help Groups in Faecal Sludge and Septage Management (FSSM) and solid waste management.

In Bhubaneswar, the Swikruti Self-Help Group took responsibility for operating and maintaining a 75-KLD Faecal Sludge Treatment Plant (FSTP) at Basuaghai. Members received orientation and technical and managerial training before taking up their responsibilities.

For Meghna Sahoo, President of Swikruti, the transformation is deeply personal. “Now, we can proudly embrace our identity and participate in the professional space,” she says. She speaks of the pride she feels when members of her group explain their work to students and visitors from national and international institutions. The significance lies not only in the job itself, but in what the job makes possible: professional identity, confidence and recognition.

The Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation has also brought transgender groups into the operation and maintenance of seven cesspool vehicles. Drivers and helpers are to be engaged with minimum applicable wages. They will also receive training on health, hygiene, personal protective equipment, and desludging protocols. Odisha's pioneering move to expand livelihood options to transgenders has won many accolades. It has set the ball rolling for others to follow, showing how inclusive participation can pave the way for better sanitation.

The Deeper Meaning of Swachhata

These stories show that Swachhata can do more than create cleaner surroundings. It can open doors to livelihoods, participation, and recognition. The real transformation lies not only in what happens to waste, but in what becomes possible for the people who manage it. When people once pushed to the margins find a place at the heart of Swachhata, cleanliness takes on a deeper meaning. It becomes a shared effort, shaped by dignity, opportunity and a sense of belonging.

Ministry of Jal Shakti

item.title: Defence Accounts Department to Celebrate 279th Annual Day
item.description:
The Defence Accounts Department (DAD) will celebrate its 279th Annual Day on October 1, 2026, in New Delhi. Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh will grace the celebrations at Dr. D.S. Kothari Auditorium, DRDO Bhawan.
On the occasion, Raksha Mantri is scheduled to launch various IT initiatives of DAD. These include the integration of the Indian Army Financial Information System (IAFIS) with the Department’s SAKSHAM platform, the revamped National Compilation System (NCS) for the Ministry…
item.content:encoded:
The Defence Accounts Department (DAD) will celebrate its 279th Annual Day on October 1, 2026, in New Delhi. Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh will grace the celebrations at Dr. D.S. Kothari Auditorium, DRDO Bhawan.

On the occasion, Raksha Mantri is scheduled to launch various IT initiatives of DAD. These include the integration of the Indian Army Financial Information System (IAFIS) with the Department’s SAKSHAM platform, the revamped National Compilation System (NCS) for the Ministry of Defence and the Payment Routing and Integrated System Management (PRISM) Platform for introducing Treasury-Single Account Payments in the Ministry of Defence.

Raksha Mantri will also release a number of publications, including the Comprehensive Statistical Handbook on Defence Expenditure (COSHE) 2026, Raksha Lekha Bharati, the Department’s in-house Hindi magazine, and the Market Intelligence Report 2025-2026.

A short film on the flagship defence pensions system - SPARSH (System for Pension Administration (Raksha)), is also scheduled to be released on the occasion. In addition, the Raksha Mantri Awards for Excellence 2026 will be conferred upon officers and staff of the Department for their exemplary performance and contribution towards implementing key initiatives of the Ministry of Defence and DAD.

Tracing its origins to the appointment of the Military Pay Master in 1747, the Defence Accounts Department has continuously evolved to meet the changing requirements of the Defence Forces and the Ministry of Defence. Over the years, DAD has played a significant role in providing services in the areas of Internal Audit, Accounting, Financial Advice and Defence Pensions Management.

item.title: Prof Neelima Satyam nominated for Prestigious Devendra Lal Memorial Medal
item.description:
Internationally recognised geotechnical engineer and Earth scientist Professor Neelima Satyam has been nominated for the prestigious Devendra Lal Memorial Medal of the American Geophysical Union (AGU) for her contributions to landslide hazard assessment, geotechnical engineering, seismic microzonation and disaster-resilient infrastructure. Prof Neelima, working as Professor in Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Madhya Pradesh, hails from Chittoor in Andhra Pradesh.
The Devendra…
item.content:encoded:
Internationally recognised geotechnical engineer and Earth scientist Professor Neelima Satyam has been nominated for the prestigious Devendra Lal Memorial Medal of the American Geophysical Union (AGU) for her contributions to landslide hazard assessment, geotechnical engineering, seismic microzonation and disaster-resilient infrastructure. Prof Neelima, working as Professor in Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Madhya Pradesh, hails from Chittoor in Andhra Pradesh. 

The Devendra Lal Memorial Medal, established in the name of renowned geophysicist Professor Devendra Lal, whose pioneering work established the use of cosmogenic isotopes as tracers in Earth science research, is awarded annually to an early- or mid-career scientist for outstanding research in Earth and space sciences. 

Professor Neelima Satyam's research integrates geotechnical engineering, geomorphology, remote sensing, real-time sensing, geospatial analytics and artificial intelligence to improve the understanding, monitoring and prediction of landslides and other geohazards.

Her work covers landslide susceptibility mapping, rainfall-threshold analysis, debris-flow characterisation and modelling, hydro-geotechnical assessment and sensor-based early-warning systems. Her research has contributed to the development of operational monitoring and early-warning frameworks in landslide-prone mountainous regions, supporting disaster-management authorities in preparedness and response to rainfall-induced slope failures.

She has also made significant contributions to seismic microzonation and earthquake hazard assessment through high-resolution shear-wave velocity profiling, site-response analysis and geotechnical hazard mapping. These studies have supported hazard-informed infrastructure planning and development.

A major aspect of Prof Neelima’s work has been translating scientific research into engineering practice. She has contributed to national technical standards and committees dealing with hill-area development, soil and foundation engineering, roads, tunnels, embankments, drainage, ground improvement and disaster management.

IIT इंदौर में सिविल इंजीनियरिंग विभाग की प्रोफेसर डॉ. नीलिमा सत्यम जी को American Geophysical Union Award द्वारा प्रतिष्ठित अंतरराष्ट्रीय सम्मान के लिए हार्दिक बधाई।

अपने उत्कृष्ट शोध एवं योगदान से आपने शिक्षा और विज्ञान के क्षेत्र में विशेष पहचान बनाई है। उज्ज्वल भविष्य के…

— Office of Dr. Mohan Yadav (@drmohanoffice51) September 27, 2026

Prof Neelima’s scholarly contributions include more than 140 peer-reviewed publications, patents and international collaborative research projects. She has also played an important role in mentoring researchers, professional training, scientific outreach and capacity building in developing regions.

The nomination recognises her sustained contributions to advancing Earth and geotechnical sciences and translating scientific knowledge into practical approaches for disaster-risk reduction and resilient infrastructure.

The medal recipient receives an engraved medal, lifetime membership of AGU, induction into the AGU College of Fellows, and recognition and an opportunity to present at the AGU annual meeting in the year of the award.

The study projects that the Ayush services…
item.content:encoded:
The Ayush services sector has emerged as one of India’s fastest-growing service sectors, with its economic contribution estimated at US$36.92 billion in FY2024-25, according to a new study by the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS). Registering a 16.91 per cent CAGR since FY2022-23, the sector is increasingly contributing to India’s economic growth through healthcare, wellness, employment generation and Medical Value Travel. The study projects that the Ayush services economy could scale to US$216–318 billion by 2047, underlining its significant potential to contribute to the Viksit Bharat @2047 vision. The Report was formally released during the 11th Ayurveda Day celebrations in Nagpur on 23rd September.

Shri Prataprao Jadhav, Union Minister of State (IC) for Ayush and Minister of State for Health & Family Welfare, emphasised that the findings mark a significant milestone in recognising the Ayush sector's economic potential. The Minister stated, “The findings of this landmark study affirm that Ayush is not merely a cultural inheritance but a dynamic and high-growth engine of India’s economy. The Ayush sector is poised to play an increasingly important role in healthcare, wellness, employment and global economic engagement, while contributing to our vision of a healthy and self-reliant India.”

Secretary, Ministry of Ayush Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha stated, “For the first time, the economic contribution of the Ayush services sector has been measured through a nationally scaled, establishment-level survey covering all major Ayush systems. The report provides a robust evidence base to guide future investment, policy planning and reforms.”

Professor Sachin Kumar Sharma, Director General, RIS, highlighted, “This study marks an important step in building an evidence-based understanding of India’s Ayush services economy. Based on a nationally scaled survey of 15,914 establishments across all six Ayush systems, the findings show that an economy of US$36.92 billion, growing at close to 17 per cent annually and supporting 1.76 million livelihoods, is no longer a peripheral sector but a dynamic, knowledge-based service economy.”

According to the study, the Ayush services economy was estimated at US$36.92 billion in FY25, registering a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 16.91 per cent since FY23. The findings underline the emergence of Ayush services as a significant and rapidly growing segment of India’s services economy, with substantial potential for further expansion through organised healthcare delivery, wellness services, quality infrastructure and global outreach.

The study shows that clinics and day-care centres constitute the core of the Ayush services economy, together accounting for more than 71 per cent of total sectoral revenue. Standalone clinics generated an estimated US$16.21 billion, while day-care centres contributed US$10.13 billion. Ayurveda remained the largest individual system, accounting for US$17.73 billion, or nearly 48 per cent of the sector’s total revenue.

The report also highlights the growing economic significance of the Ayush-based wellness segment, including yoga centres, spas and resorts offering Ayush-based services. The segment recorded a 21.29 per cent CAGR, with yoga centres registering around 75 per cent growth in revenue over two years, reflecting rising demand for preventive health, wellness and holistic care services.

The study finds that Ayush services sector has emerged as a significant source of employment. Sector directly supports 1.76 million livelihoods, with more than one million jobs concentrated in local and standalone clinics. Women account for 43 per cent of the overall Ayush services workforce, with female participation exceeding 50 per cent in several organised segments. Women constitute over 60 per cent of the workforce in wellness settings (spas and resorts) offering Ayush-based services, 58 per cent in educational institutions, 57 per cent in day-care centres and 53 per cent in hospitals.

The study further points to the growing potential of Ayush in Medical Value Travel (MVT). The sector generated an estimated US$1.77 billion in MVT revenue in FY25. While international patients account for only around 5 per cent of patient volumes, they contribute an estimated 15–25 per cent of hospital-segment revenues. The study notes that Ayush therapeutic programmes, including Panchakarma and residential Yoga, are associated with longer patient stays, with an average length of stay ranging from 5 to 11 days.

Digital visibility and quality accreditation are also emerging as important factors in attracting international patients. According to the study, establishments with a dedicated functional website have 3.6 times higher odds of attracting international patients, while recognised quality accreditation such as NABH or ISO is associated with a doubling of such odds.

Looking ahead, the study projects significant growth potential for the sector as India advances towards Viksit Bharat @2047. The Ayush services economy could expand from the estimated US$36.92 billion in FY25 to US$216 billion–US$318 billion by 2047, subject to the strengthening of infrastructure, quality systems, skills, digital capabilities and international market access.

The study outlines a strategic pathway backed by an analysis through four pillars: — knowledge  value chain of Ayush; enterprise and institutional capabilities;  global competitiveness and Medical Value Travel;  innovation through digital technologies and Artificial Intelligence. It also emphasises the need for wider quality accreditation, digital health records, workforce skilling, international readiness and responsible adoption of emerging technologies.

The findings reinforce the expanding role of Ayush not only as a healthcare and wellness ecosystem but also as a contributor to employment generation, entrepreneurship, services-led economic growth and India’s growing global engagement in traditional and complementary medicine.

The RIS study provides an evidence-based assessment of the evolving Ayush services landscape and identifies opportunities for strengthening the sector’s contribution to India’s healthcare, wellness and economic development priorities in the years ahead.

SR/SV/SG

item.description:
The Department of Food and Public Distribution (DFPD), along with its subordinate/attached offices and PSUs, has started preparations for the Special Campaign for Disposal of Pending Matters 6 (SCDPM 6).
This year, special focus is being given to the collection, segregation and disposal of e-waste, along with cleanliness, disposal of pending matters and better use of office space.
The preparatory phase is being undertaken from 15 September to 30 September 2026 . During this…
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Food and Public Distribution (DFPD), along with its subordinate/attached offices and PSUs, has started preparations for the Special Campaign for Disposal of Pending Matters 6 (SCDPM 6).

This year, special focus is being given to the collection, segregation and disposal of e-waste, along with cleanliness, disposal of pending matters and better use of office space.

The preparatory phase is being undertaken from 15 September to 30 September 2026. During this period, DFPD and its attached/subordinate offices and PSUs, including Food Corporation of India (FCI), Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) and Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA), are reviewing physical and electronic files, identifying e-waste, scrap and unserviceable items, and taking necessary steps for their proper disposal. The initiative aims to promote responsible waste management practices.

 

 

Key Targets

As part of the preparatory phase, the following targets have been identified up to 28 September 2026:

  • 947 sites identified for intensive cleanliness drives at offices, depots and warehouses.
  • 22,635 sq. ft. of space identified for freeing up through disposal of clutter and obsolete materials.
  • 3,660 physical files identified for review and weeding out as per record retention rules.
  • 3,534 e-files identified for closure to strengthen digital record management.
  • 439 e-waste items identified for collection, segregation and disposal.

The Department is holding regular review meetings with nodal officers and senior officials to monitor the progress of the campaign. The activities include cleanliness drives, disposal of pending matters, freeing up of space, record management and proper disposal of e-waste.

The Department of Food and Public Distribution is closely monitoring the preparatory activities for effective implementation of Special Campaign 6 from 2 October to 31 October 2026.

Through Special Campaign 6, DFPD and its attached/subordinate offices and PSUs aim to promote cleaner and better-organised workplaces, reduce pendency, strengthen record management, optimise available space and ensure responsible management of e-waste.

***

IA/ RP

item.title: Beyond Wastewater: Turning Used Water into a Resource
item.description: In growing cities, the water cycle does not end when water is used. What flows away from homes, businesses and neighbourhoods does not have to become waste. With the right systems, used water can be collected, treated, recycled and returned to productive use. This shift is shaping a new approach to urban sanitation under the Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban (SBM-U) . At its heart is Used Water Management (UWM) , which focuses on treating used water, preventing untreated sewage from reaching water…
item.content:encoded:
In growing cities, the water cycle does not end when water is used. What flows away from homes, businesses and neighbourhoods does not have to become waste. With the right systems, used water can be collected, treated, recycled and returned to productive use. This shift is shaping a new approach to urban sanitation under the Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban (SBM-U). At its heart is Used Water Management (UWM), which focuses on treating used water, preventing untreated sewage from reaching water bodies, and enabling safe reuse. Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) are central to this process, turning wastewater management into an opportunity to protect natural resources and recover water for further use.

This approach is reinforced through the Water Plus certification, which provides cities with guidelines for managing wastewater generated by households and commercial establishments. It requires wastewater to meet satisfactory treatment standards before being discharged into the environment. The focus extends beyond treatment infrastructure to how cities plan and manage their water resources. Urban Local Bodies are being empowered to formulate long-term, city-level plans for wastewater reuse. Clearly defined responsibilities and technological advancements are helping cities improve the efficiency and effectiveness of treatment systems. The Open Defecation Free (ODF) ++ protocols further strengthen this approach by assessing the safe management and treatment of entire sewage, including faecal sludge and septage.

Together, these measures are laying the foundation for sustainable sanitation and a circular economy, where used water can be managed as a resource. Under SBM 2.0, projects worth ₹11,785 crore have been approved for setting up sewage treatment plants in small cities. These projects will add 4,900 million litres per day (MLD) of treatment capacity, expanding the infrastructure needed for effective used water management.

Where Used Water Finds a Second Life

The management of used water is evolving beyond conventional treatment and disposal. Different cities are developing approaches that match their infrastructure, water needs and local conditions. In the process, treated water is finding applications in agriculture, horticulture, industry, road cleaning and lake rejuvenation. The experiences of cities like Jaipur, Indore, Surat and Navi Mumbai highlight some of these varied approaches.

Jaipur: Engineering Water Reuse at Scale

Water Treatment at Dehlawas Plant

Built over 22.50 hectares during 2020–23, the Dehlawas Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) in Jaipur has the highest sewage treatment capacity in Rajasthan, at 215 MLD. Wastewater is effectively treated and converted into a reusable resource, thereby promoting the concepts of circular economy and water conservation. This high-technology plant is fully automated through a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system.

The plant discharging treated water into the Dravyavati River

Jaipur STP is currently equipped with a highly efficient Sequencing Batch Reactor (SBR). In this process, wastewater passes through a Parshall flume, primary clarifier and basin before reaching the chlorine tank. It is then converted into clean water. Solid waste is separated using primary sludge thickeners and screw press machines. Once treated at the STP, wastewater becomes a valuable resource once again. It is being reused for irrigation and various industrial processes, a practice known as wastewater recycling, which is also an economically viable option. At present, a portion of the treated water is being supplied to a nearby colony for gardening and other purposes. The remaining clean water is discharged into the Dravyavati River, while measures are being taken to ensure that untreated wastewater does not enter the river. A green area has also been developed around the plant, with more than 30,000 plants adding to the greenery of the site.  

Indore: Leading the Water Plus Journey

Indore’s transformation in used water management began with a simple goal: keep untreated wastewater out of the environment. This approach helped the city become the first to receive Water+ Certification. Its practices demonstrated how sustainable sanitation and used water management could work at the city level. The model has also encouraged several smaller cities to pursue similar approaches.

Today, no untreated wastewater flows through Indore’s rivers or its natural and man-made stormwater drains. By 2020, the city had 7 decentralised STPs alongside 3 existing centralised STPs. It had also laid more than 200 kilometres of piped network for carrying treated wastewater. Indore simultaneously strengthened measures for conserving both groundwater and surface water. In 2022, more than 1.25 lakh rainwater harvesting units were installed across residential and non-residential areas. The installations were completed within a span of just four months. Treated wastewater is now used for water gardens, roadside plantations and horticulture. It is also used for washing roads and cleaning sewer machines.

Surat: Making Wastewater an Economic Resource

Water Treatment Plants in Surat 

Surat has taken the idea of wastewater reuse further by treating it as a resource with economic value. The Surat Municipal Corporation has established four tertiary treatment plants with a combined installed capacity of 116 MLD. The plants have helped reduce dependence on freshwater resources. Treated wastewater is reused across several non-potable applications in the city. These include industrial use, lake rejuvenation, agriculture, mass plantation, sewer cleaning, etc., through direct service lines and tanker filling stations. The city has 170 sewer-cleaning machines, including equipment based on Latest Advanced Robotic Technology. These machines are used for cleaning and maintaining the sewerage system.

Navi Mumbai: Reuse Built into City Services

Sewage Treatment in Navi Mumbai

Navi Mumbai’s Water+ journey has combined treatment infrastructure with extensive reuse of treated water. It is the only city in Maharashtra to achieve a five-star rating and Water+ Certification. The city upgraded its sewage treatment technology and designed its STPs for a population of 30 lakh. Its pumping stations were also upgraded to reduce energy costs. These stations transfer sewage generated to the STPs. Preventive maintenance of the sewer network was undertaken to avoid hotspots. Navi Mumbai has achieved 100% mechanised cleaning of sewer lines and septic tanks. Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation centrally monitors all septic tanks through Level Transmitters installed across the city. More than 30% of treated water is reused in over 30 city gardens. It is also used to wash solid-waste vehicles, compactors and city transport buses. Sprinklers and road dividers also use treated water, reducing dependence on freshwater.

Tirupati: A Revenue Model for Treated Water

Tirupati has developed a self-sustaining model for operating a sewage treatment plant at Thukivakam. The city has also been declared Water Plus. Built at a cost of ₹19 crore, the STP has an installed capacity of 50 MLD. It serves 1,04,057 households across the city. Of the treated water, 24 MLD is reused for various purposes. The plant sells 5 MLD of treated used water to Srikalahasthi Pipes Ltd. With this, the plant is able to generate a net revenue of Rs. 6 Lakhs per month. Another 18 MLD of treated used water is supplied free of cost to farmers for agriculture. The ULB also reuses a portion for road and street cleaning. Treated water is further used for watering road medians, parks and gardens across the city. These measures help maximise the reuse of treated water. Tirupati’s approach combines wastewater reuse with a revenue-generating model for sustainable STP operations.

Water Treatment Plant in Tirupati

A Shift in the Urban Water Story

The growing focus on used water management is changing how cities approach their water needs. Treatment is no longer only about preventing pollution. It is also about recovering water for productive use. Treated water is finding new uses in irrigation, industry, horticulture and everyday urban services. As more cities strengthen treatment capacity and develop reuse systems, urban water management is becoming more circular and resource-efficient. This shift helps build cleaner sanitation systems while making better use of every available water resource.

 Reference

Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

item.title: India’s indigenous technology push gains momentum as HD Kumaraswamy unveils MHI Industry Accelerator Impact Report at Navigyaan 2026
item.description:
Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel, H. D. Kumaraswamy on Wednesday unveiled and digitally launched the Impact Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) Industry Accelerator Project at Navigyaan 2026 in New Delhi, marking an important milestone in the development and advancement of indigenous technologies for India’s mobility and manufacturing sectors.
Addressing the gathering, H.D. Kumaraswamy said the event marked the conclusion of the MHI Industry…
item.content:encoded:
Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel, H. D. Kumaraswamy on Wednesday unveiled and digitally launched the Impact Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) Industry Accelerator Project at Navigyaan 2026 in New Delhi, marking an important milestone in the development and advancement of indigenous technologies for India’s mobility and manufacturing sectors.

 

Addressing the gathering, H.D. Kumaraswamy said the event marked the conclusion of the MHI Industry Accelerator Project and highlighted the importance of building domestic technological and manufacturing capabilities.

“The Government of India under the visionary leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modiji, has placed strong emphasis on building domestic technological and manufacturing capabilities,” he said.

The Minister said that the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat requires India to move beyond being a large market for advanced technologies and develop the capacity to manufacture and export them.

“The vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat calls for an India that is not only a large market for advanced technologies, but also a country that develops, manufactures and exports those,” Kumaraswamy said.

Highlighting the scale of support extended under the Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector - Phase II, he said the scheme has a total financial outlay of ₹1,207 crore and aims to support common technology development and services infrastructure. Under the scheme, 33 projects have been approved.

The MHI Industry Accelerator Programme, one of these initiatives, provided ₹35.72 crore in Grant-in-Aid for 10 technologies, with the objective of supporting their progression from Technology Readiness Level 3 to Level 9.

Kumaraswamy noted that the technologies supported under the programme cover several areas of future mobility, including electric powertrains, high-voltage motor control and energy storage. An important outcome, he said, has been the movement of technologies from early-stage prototypes towards commercially viable products.

Emphasising the importance of collaboration in technology development, the Minister said government, industry, research institutions, academia, startups and institutions such as ARAI each have an important role in strengthening the innovation ecosystem.

“Government can provide the policy framework and targeted support. Industry brings market understanding and manufacturing capability. Research and academic institutions contribute knowledge and technology. Startups bring new ideas and agility,” he said.

He further underlined the role of institutions such as ARAI in bridging the gap between technology development, validation and industry adoption.

Kumaraswamy said that as India moves towards Viksit Bharat@2047, the focus must remain on developing capabilities within the country and taking Indian technologies to international markets.

“It is this ecosystem that we need to strengthen further. As we move towards Viksit Bharat@2047, our focus should be clear: educate, innovate, manufacture and integrate technologies in India and take Indian technologies to global markets,” he said.

The Minister also stressed that self-reliance should extend beyond import substitution and focus on developing Indian intellectual property, resilient supply chains and skilled human resources.

“The objective of self-reliance is not simply to replace imports. It is to build Indian intellectual property, supply chains and skilled human resources,” Kumaraswamy said.

 

He called for continued efforts to identify emerging technology requirements, strengthen industry-academia collaboration and develop talent capable of meeting the technological needs of the future.

Concluding his address, Kumaraswamy said India must create an ecosystem that enables innovations to move efficiently through every stage of development.

“Let us continue to build an ecosystem in which Indian innovation can move efficiently from concept to prototype, prototype to product, and product to global market,” he said.

The Minister also felicitated members of the MHI Industry Accelerator Project for their contribution towards taking technologies from development and validation to industrial application and commercialisation. The event, organised as a culmination of the MHI Industry Accelerator Project implemented by ARAI-AMTIF, brought together stakeholders from government, industry, academia, research and the technology ecosystem.

 

During the programme, Kumaraswamy visited the startup exhibition and reviewed innovations supported under the Accelerator initiative. The technologies showcased at the exhibition covered areas including electric mobility, power electronics, high-voltage systems, energy storage, predictive maintenance, sensors and advanced surface engineering.

 

***

TPJ

item.title: SECOND EDITION OF NAVAL COMMANDERS’ CONFERENCE 2026 AT NEW DELHI
item.description:
The second edition of the Naval Commanders’ Conference 2026 commenced at Nausena Bhawan , New Delhi on 29 Sep 2026 , bringing together the senior leadership of the Indian Navy, including Operational and Area Commanders, for deliberations on operational preparedness, maritime security and future capability development.
The Conference commenced with the inaugural address by Adm Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of the Naval Staff, who reviewed the prevailing maritime security environment…
item.content:encoded:
The second edition of the Naval Commanders’ Conference 2026 commenced at Nausena Bhawan, New Delhi on 29 Sep 2026, bringing together the senior leadership of the Indian Navy, including Operational and Area Commanders, for deliberations on operational preparedness, maritime security and future capability development.

The Conference commenced with the inaugural address by Adm Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of the Naval Staff, who reviewed the prevailing maritime security environment and the Indian Navy’s operational posture. He underscored the imperative of maintaining a high degree of combat readiness, agility and responsiveness while accelerating technology absorption and capability development to address contemporary and emerging challenges across the maritime domain.

Addressing the Naval Commanders, Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh underscored India’s growing strategic responsibilities in the maritime domain and the Indian Navy’s role as a First Responder and Preferred Security Partner in the Indian Ocean Region. He stressed the need to strengthen maritime surveillance, analytical capability and operational responsiveness (https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2316492&reg=3&lang=1 ).

Referring to the situation in West Asia, he highlighted the Navy’s conduct of Operation Urja Suraksha and its contribution to safeguarding India’s energy security. He also emphasised Aatmanirbharta, indigenous capability development and technology absorption, underscoring that secure seas are integral to a secure nation and a developed nation.

Gen NS Raja Subramani Chief of the Defence Staff acknowledged the Indian Navy as a strategic force multiplier and commended its sustained efforts towards technology absorption, Aatmanirbharta and safeguarding India’s energy security. He highlighted the changing character of warfare and emphasised the need for accelerated technology transformation, seamless data sharing, enhanced resilience and sustenance, underpinned by greater Jointness and integration across the Services.

Gen Dhiraj Seth, Chief of the Army Staff, also interacted with the Naval Commanders and shared perspectives on the contemporary security environment. The interaction focused on further strengthening Tri-Service synergy, interoperability and integrated responses to emerging security challenges. The discussions reinforced the need for closer coordination and continued exchange of operational lessons among the Services towards enhancing joint preparedness.

The engagements with the CDS and COAS provided an opportunity for the Naval leadership to exchange perspectives on the evolving character of warfare, capability development and the increasing importance of integrated operations in addressing emerging security challenges.

During the remaining sessions of the three-day Conference, the Naval leadership will undertake detailed deliberations on Operations, Materiel, Logistics, Human Resources, Training, force development and induction of emerging technologies. Measures to optimise force levels, strengthen combat readiness and accelerate capability development will also be reviewed.

*****

 

VM/AS

item.title: TRAI Assesses Mobile Network Quality across Sonitpur district under Assam LSA in the state of Assam
item.description: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has released findings of Independent Drive Test (IDT) conducted across Sonitpur district in the state of Assam under Assam LSA, during the month of August 2026, for information of general telecom consumers. The purpose of this drive test is to assess and verify real time quality of mobile network services (both voice & data) provided by Telecom Service Providers (TSPs). During the IDT, TRAI captures performance of TSPs for key Quality of Service…
item.content:encoded:
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has released findings of Independent Drive Test (IDT) conducted across Sonitpur district in the state of Assam under Assam LSA, during the month of August 2026, for information of general telecom consumers. The purpose of this drive test is to assess and verify real time quality of mobile network services (both voice & data) provided by Telecom Service Providers (TSPs). During the IDT, TRAI captures performance of TSPs for key Quality of Service (QoS) parameters like Coverage, Call Drop Rate (CDR), Call Setup Success Rate (CSSR), data Download (DL) and Upload (UL) throughput etc., which are then published to inform Consumers and encourage TSPs to improve their services.
These IDTs have been designed to capture on ground mobile network performance of all TSPs across diverse usages environment like cities, hotspots, public transport hubs, etc. In this type of drive testing, live data and voice sessions are established using SIM cards from all TSPs over 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G networks. Multiple advanced test handsets are used, and the sessions are monitored and analysed in real-time using advanced Software Systems. 
TRAI, through its appointed agency, conducted drive tests across City drive – 308.0 KMs, Hotspot locations - 10, Walk Test – 1.6 KMs in Assam LSA during 10th August 2026 to 13th August 2026 in Assam LSA. These tests were conducted under the supervision of the TRAI Regional Office Kolkata. The observations presented in drive test reports represent the performance of the TSPs on the area/ route under test on the day/ time of conducting the drive test.
Drive Test Route Map: The following map provides overview of drive test routes indicating City drive, Inter-operator calling, Hotspots and Walk tests, as per the legends shown on the map: -
 


Key Parameters Assessed
a)    Coverage Gap: Percentage of samples, for which signal strength observed less than the minimum prescribed signal strength for respective technology (2G/ 3G/ 4G/ 5G).
b)    Voice Services: Call Setup Success Rate (CSSR), Drop Call Rate (DCR), Call Setup Time, Call Silence Rate, Speech Quality (MOS).
c)    Call Silence Instance: Number of call silence instance occurred during the calls.
d)    Data Services: Download/ Upload Throughput, Latency, Jitter, Packet Drop Rate
    
The overall mobile network performance in parts of Sonitpur district under Assam LSA for the key parameters has been summarised below: -
a)    Coverage Gap - The signal strength observed during voice testing on the city drive test route in auto-selection mode (5G/4G/3G/2G), measured as the number of samples having poor signal strength out of the total samples collected, was 1766 / 44378 for Airtel, 18494 /41037 for BSNL, 1494/ 43999 for RJIL and 6682 / 44109 for VIL. Details of the coverage gaps have been provided in the map Annexed. 

b)    Dropped Calls - Dropped calls, measured as the number of dropped calls out of the number of successfully established calls, were 0/ 311 for Airtel, 301/ 476 for BSNL, 0/ 316 for RJIL and 8/ 312 for VIL. Details of the dropped call locations have been provided in the map Annexed.

c)    Call Silence Instance - Call silence instances, measured as the total number of silence instances observed for > 3 seconds out of the total calls established, were 13/ 309 for Airtel, 7/ 253 for BSNL, 7/ 309 for RJIL and 8/ 310 for VIL. Details of the call silence instance locations have been provided in the map Annexed.

d)    Data Download and Upload Throughput:

i)    Data Download performance (Overall): Average download speed was observed as 116.11Mbps for Airtel (5G/4G), 11.72 Mbps for BSNL (4G/2G), 221.18 Mbps for RJIL (5G/4G) and 20.04 Mbps for VIL (4G/2G). Detail of Download throughput has been provided in the map Annexed.

ii)    Data Upload performance (Overall): Average upload speed was observed as 21.09 Mbps for Airtel (5G/4G), 4.32 Mbps for BSNL (4G/ 2G), 15.98 Mbps for RJIL (5G/4G) and 6.69 Mbps for VIL (4G/2G). Detail of Upload throughput has been provided in the map Annexed.

Locations of Dropped Calls and Call Silence instances can be seen by clicking red dot on the map Annexed.

Details of drive test route and area covered during the IDT is as under: -
a)      City - The areas covered in the city drive are (i) Da-Parbatia Gaon (ii) Gutlong Gaon, (iii) Parmai Gauli Gaon,(iv)  Dhalaibil,  (v) No.1 Malijan, (vi) Tezpur, (vi) Kumar Gaon, (vii) Uhani Pathar Batabari, Dekeri Gaon,  (viii) No.1 Thakurbari T.E, Bindukuri Gaon, Rangamati Gaon, (ix) Sonabil, Nepali Basti Gaon, (x) Thelamara, (xi)Natun Pam Gaon, (xii) Kukura-Khaiti and Dhekiajuli Bagan etc.

b)   Hotspot - The hot spot locations, capturing stationary user experience, are (i) ASTC Bus Stand - Mahabhairab – Tezpur, (ii) Dhekiajuli Block Development Office – Dhekiajuli, (iii) District Court Tezpur - Mahatma Gandhi Rd - Mahabhairab – Tezpur, (iv) Narengkati Higher Secondary School - No.2 - Singimari Gaon, (v) North Eastern Regional Institute of Water and Land Management - Dolabari – Tezpur, (vi) St. Xaviers College - Goraimari – Tezpur, (vii) Tezpur Head Post Office - Mahabhairab – Tezpur, (viii) Tezpur Medical College and Hospital - Niz - Bihaguri Gaon – Tezpur, (ix) Tezpur University - Napaam – Tezpur, (x) Udmari Gaon Panchayat - Balipara
c)  Walk Test - The walk tests conducted during 12th to 13th August 2026, are (i) North Jamuguri BPHC/CHC - Panigaon – Dhalaibil, (ii) Rangapara North Junction - No.1 - Thakurbari T.E. capturing mobile network behaviour in crowded pedestrian environments. 
The findings of this IDT report have been shared with respective TSPs for taking further necessary action at their end. Detailed reports of IDT are made available on the TRAI website at www.trai.gov.in. For any clarification or additional information, an email can be sent to adv.kolkata@trai.gov.in or Regional Office of TRAI at Kolkata RO can be contacted on telephone no.  +91-33-22361401.

item.content:encoded:
From Toxic to Valuable: Cleaning Wastewater, Finding Treasure

We generally throw away a broken camera lens, earphones, or an old phone that has stopped working and is beyond repair, as they feel useless when non-functional. However, these objects hide within them rare earth elements (REEs) that have applications in magnets, superconductivity, optics, and batteries, among others. When such objects become part of water, recovering REEs becomes difficult.

On the other hand, industrial activities can introduce toxic metals such as lead, cadmium, nickel and manganese into the same water. The challenge is no longer simply how to remove these unwanted, harmful metal pollutants from water, but also efficiently recapturing the valuable REEs.

What if a single strategy could help address both issues? As an effort in this direction, researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar (IITGN), the University of Cambridge, and the University of Birmingham have collaboratively developed a protocol using a class of highly porous materials called metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). They can efficiently capture toxic metals from water as well as recover valuable REEs from waste streams. Published in Nature Protocols, the study provides a framework for designing, characterising and deploying MOFs in water remediation as well as circular resource applications with respect to real-world conditions.

An Intelligent Filter

Think of the MOF as a molecular fishing net. Its countless pores spread out a vast catching surface, while specially designed chemical sites act like hooks that can latch on to particular metals. The researchers tuned this net such that it preferentially traps the metals they are looking for. It is like identifying and specifically picking red and green coloured marbles from a bucket containing hundreds of marbles in different colours.

Some MOFs can have internal surface areas of up to 7,000 square metres per gram. To put that number in perspective, one gram may look like a tiny pinch of powder, but inside it is a surface area comparable to an entire football field!

This huge internal surface makes MOFs attractive as adsorbents. In simple terms, they function as materials that arrest substances on their surfaces. While conventional methods such as precipitation, coagulation and flocculation can be useful for water treatment, they are generally sensitive to pH, with optimal removal confined to narrow ranges. Broadly speaking, precipitation lets heavy impurities settle out, coagulation makes impurities clump together, and flocculation makes small impurity clumps collide and grow into larger clusters that can be separated.

These approaches also require large infrastructure and generate large amounts of sludge, a thick, muddy waste that then has to be handled and disposed of. Other processes, such as the electrochemical treatment, have high economic and environmental costs.

Adsorption offers an effective alternative that is simple to operate, with broad applicability and effectiveness at low contaminant concentrations. Since it focuses on the extent of affinity of the target metals to the tailored surface, it has the potential to remove 90 - 99% of contaminants like a highly selective filter! Using adsorption-based approaches also avoids generating secondary contaminants and can be regenerated and reused. Within this space, MOFs stand out for their exceptional design flexibility in capturing and recovering metals.

Beyond the Laboratory

In the real world, industrial effluents, which are waste products discharged from manufacturing, mining, and chemical processing facilities into water bodies, contain not just one but many metals, along with other contaminants like pesticides, detergents, and organic pollutants.

The protocol details a methodology which can be used to employ MOFs as an adsorbent for the recovery and removal of metals under controlled conditions. The protocol features testing in complex real-world scenarios. For example, removal and recovery were evaluated using wastewater that is alkaline (pH ~ 8.5), turbid, and high in dissolved solid impurities. The method was also tested in artificial seawater and e-waste-derived samples. The workflow developed in this study can be applied to similar adsorbents and other contaminants.

“For me, the most interesting aspect was observing the MOF in our protocol demonstrate substantial adsorption capacities,” said Dhruv Menon (BTech, IITGN). He added, “The experiments showed that one gram of the copper-based MOF could capture nearly half a gram of lead (490 mg/g), and roughly a quarter of a gram each of cadmium (264 mg/g) and manganese (226 mg/g). For rare-earth elements, it could capture around one-third of a gram per gram of material (351 mg/g of neodymium, 343 mg/g of yttrium, 335 mg/g of dysprosium, 337 mg/g of terbium and 345 mg/g of europium).” Mr Menon is currently a doctoral student in the Department of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology at the University of Cambridge.

Towards Sustainability

As explained by Prof Superb Misra, “There is a need for approaches that can solve multiple environmental challenges simultaneously. Our focus was on engineering the performance of MOFs to employ them for environmental remediation applications. That said, it is crucial to understand that controlled batch experiments cannot fully predict behaviours in complex wastewater. There is a need to look at factors like large-scale fabrication, cost analyses, MOF life-cycle assessment and regulatory testing,” Dr Misra is the Jibaben Patel Chair Professor in the Department of Materials Engineering, IITGN, and the Principal Investigator at the Bio Nano Materials Group.

Other team members involved in this study included Prathmesh Bhadane (PhD, IITGN; Postdoctoral fellow, IIT Bombay), Priya Mahato (doctoral student, IITGN), Prateek Goyal (PhD, IITGN), Dr Iseult Lynch (Professor, School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Birmingham), and Dr Swaroop Chakraborty (NERC Fellow, University of Birmingham). 

This research aligns with the Government of India’s Critical Mineral Recycling Incentive Scheme, as part of the National Critical Mineral Mission, to develop domestic recycling capacity for separating and producing critical minerals from secondary sources, including growing volumes of e-waste and battery waste. IIT Gandhinagar is a partner in the Centre of Excellence on National Critical Minerals Mission hosted at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad. The findings are also in alignment with the UK-India Technology Security Initiative, which involves collaboration on sustainable extraction and recovery of critical minerals from end-of-life waste streams. They also coincide with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 6, 9 and 12, focused on clean water and sanitation, industry and innovation, and responsible consumption and production.

*****
